How neutral-mass voting works

2026-11-10

Source: vignettes/neutral-mass-voting.qmd

The example

This vignette walks through the annotation of one feature group step by step, using the low-level functions that annotateAdducts() is built from. The group holds the ions of 2-furoylglycine (C7H7NO4, M = 169.0375 Da), a marker of coffee intake, measured in positive mode in a coffee intervention study. All eight features elute within 0.2 s and their intensities correlate across the study samples, so groupFeatures() put them in one group.

library(IonFamilies)

mz <- c(95.0124, 124.0392, 152.0342, 170.0445, 171.0496, 192.0275,
        377.0300, 393.0019)
int <- c(71.6, 81.4, 49.8, 100, 4.33, 11.3, 1.76, 1.82)
grp <- rep("FG.1", length(mz))

Step 1: isotopes

Heavy isotopologues are not adducts, so they are found first and left out of the voting. MetaboCoreUtils::isotopologues() checks that the mass difference fits an isotope step and that the intensity ratio is plausible for a molecule of that mass.

iso <- annotateIsotopes(mz, IsotopologueParam(), intensity = int,
                        groups = grp)
data.frame(mz, int, iso)
#>         mz    int       iso
#> 1  95.0124  71.60          
#> 2 124.0392  81.40          
#> 3 152.0342  49.80          
#> 4 170.0445 100.00   [1][M]+
#> 5 171.0496   4.33 [1][M+1]+
#> 6 192.0275  11.30          
#> 7 377.0300   1.76          
#> 8 393.0019   1.82

m/z 171.050 is the ¹³C isotopologue of m/z 170.045 (4 % of its intensity, about what seven carbons give).

Step 2: implied neutral masses

A rule describes how an ion is formed from nmol neutral molecules: its charge and the mass that is added or lost (massdiff). Inverting it gives the neutral mass a feature would have if it were that ion:

M=|z|⋅m/z−ΔmnmolM = \frac{|z| \cdot m/z - \Delta m}{n_{mol}}

rules <- defaultAdductRules("positive")
some <- rules[rules$name %in% c("[M+H]+", "[M+Na]+", "[M+H-H2O]+",
                                "[M+H-HCOOH]+", "[2M+K]+"), ]
some[, c("name", "nmol", "charge", "massdiff", "quasi", "ips")]
#>            name nmol charge   massdiff quasi  ips
#> 1        [M+H]+    1      1   1.007276     1 1.00
#> 13      [M+Na]+    1      1  22.989218     1 1.00
#> 23      [2M+K]+    2      1  38.963158     0 0.75
#> 62 [M+H-HCOOH]+    1      1 -44.998203     0 0.75
#> 64   [M+H-H2O]+    1      1 -17.003288     1 0.75
round(impliedMasses(mz, some), 4)
#>        [M+H]+  [M+Na]+  [2M+K]+ [M+H-HCOOH]+ [M+H-H2O]+
#> [1,]  94.0051  72.0232  28.0246     140.0106   112.0157
#> [2,] 123.0319 101.0500  42.5380     169.0374   141.0425
#> [3,] 151.0269 129.0450  56.5355     197.0324   169.0375
#> [4,] 169.0372 147.0553  65.5407     215.0427   187.0478
#> [5,] 170.0423 148.0604  66.0432     216.0478   188.0529
#> [6,] 191.0202 169.0383  76.5322     237.0257   209.0308
#> [7,] 376.0227 354.0408 169.0334     422.0282   394.0333
#> [8,] 391.9946 370.0127 177.0194     438.0001   410.0052

Read the table column by column. The value 169.037 appears for m/z 170.045 as [M+H]+, for 192.028 as [M+Na]+, for 152.034 as [M+H-H2O]+, for 124.039 as [M+H-HCOOH]+ and for 377.030 as [2M+K]+. Five features agree on one neutral mass.

Step 3: voting

neutralMassVote() automates that reading for all rules:

  1. Every feature is tried as every quasi-molecular ion (rules with quasi == 1, such as [M+H]+ and [M+Na]+). Each try is an anchor and gives a candidate neutral mass.
  2. A candidate becomes a hypothesis when at least one other feature is explained by some rule as an ion of the same mass (within ppm + mzabs).
  3. Hypotheses found from different anchors but with the same members are merged.
  4. Hypotheses are ranked by the summed rule score (ips, higher for common ions) and then by the intensity they explain.
keep <- !isIsotopologue(iso)
votes <- neutralMassVote(mz[keep], int[keep], rules)
votes$mz <- mz[keep][votes$feature]
head(votes[, c("hypothesis", "M", "n_ions", "score", "mz", "adduct")], 12)
#>    hypothesis         M n_ions score       mz
#> 1           1 169.03722      5  4.25 170.0445
#> 2           1 169.03722      5  4.25 192.0275
#> 3           1 169.03722      5  4.25 377.0300
#> 4           1 169.03722      5  4.25 124.0392
#> 5           1 169.03722      5  4.25 152.0342
#> 6           2 151.02692      3  2.25 152.0342
#> 7           2 151.02692      3  2.25 124.0392
#> 8           2 151.02692      3  2.25  95.0124
#> 9           3 147.05528      3  2.25 170.0445
#> 10          3 147.05528      3  2.25 192.0275
#> 11          3 147.05528      3  2.25  95.0124
#> 12          4  94.00512      2  2.00  95.0124
#>                                   adduct
#> 1                                 [M+H]+
#> 2                                [M+Na]+
#> 3                                [2M+K]+
#> 4                           [M+H-HCOOH]+
#> 5                             [M+H-H2O]+
#> 6                                 [M+H]+
#> 7                              [M+H-CO]+
#> 8  [M+H - O=C=NCH3 (methyl isocyanate)]+
#> 9                                [M+Na]+
#> 10                            [M+2Na-H]+
#> 11                    [M+H-NH3-H2O-H2O]+
#> 12                                [M+H]+

Hypothesis 1 is furoylglycine with five supporting ions. The later hypotheses are coincidences: with 159 rules, most pairs of m/z values can be connected by some pair of rules.

Step 4: keep all hypotheses or only the best?

CAMERA reported, for each feature, only hypotheses that did not conflict with better ones. bestHypotheses() reproduces that choice:

hints <- annotateAdducts(mz, AdductVoteParam(), intensity = int,
                         groups = grp, exclude = !keep)
best <- bestHypotheses(hints)
best$mz <- mz[best$feature]
best[, c("mz", "M", "adduct", "n_ions")]
#>         mz        M       adduct n_ions
#> 1 124.0392 169.0372 [M+H-HCOOH]+      5
#> 2 152.0342 169.0372   [M+H-H2O]+      5
#> 3 170.0445 169.0372       [M+H]+      5
#> 4 192.0275 169.0372      [M+Na]+      5
#> 5 377.0300 169.0372      [2M+K]+      5

IonFamilies keeps all hypotheses by default, ranked per feature. A true annotation that ranks second for a feature is then still visible. Missing a true relationship costs more than showing an extra suggestion, because annotations are hints to be checked. nBest limits how many are written to text:

data.frame(mz, iso,
           best_only = formatAdducts(hints, nBest = 1, nFeatures = length(mz)),
           top_three = formatAdducts(hints, nBest = 3, nFeatures = length(mz)))
#>         mz       iso                                     best_only
#> 1  95.0124           [M+H - O=C=NCH3 (methyl isocyanate)]+ 151.027
#> 2 124.0392                                    [M+H-HCOOH]+ 169.037
#> 3 152.0342                                      [M+H-H2O]+ 169.037
#> 4 170.0445   [1][M]+                                [M+H]+ 169.037
#> 5 171.0496 [1][M+1]+                                              
#> 6 192.0275                                         [M+Na]+ 169.037
#> 7 377.0300                                         [2M+K]+ 169.037
#> 8 393.0019                                          [M+K]+ 354.041
#>                                                                                top_three
#> 1 [M+H - O=C=NCH3 (methyl isocyanate)]+ 151.027 [M+H-NH3-H2O-H2O]+ 147.055 [M+H]+ 94.005
#> 2                        [M+H-HCOOH]+ 169.037 [M+H-CO]+ 151.027 [M+H-H2O-HCOOH]+ 187.048
#> 3                                [M+H-H2O]+ 169.037 [M+H]+ 151.027 [M+H-(H2O)2]+ 187.048
#> 4                                      [M+H]+ 169.037 [M+Na]+ 147.055 [M+H-H2O]+ 187.048
#> 5                                                                                       
#> 6                                 [M+Na]+ 169.037 [M+2Na-H]+ 147.055 [M+Na+K-H]+ 131.081
#> 7                                         [2M+K]+ 169.037 [4M+H]+ 94.005 [M+Na]+ 354.041
#> 8                                                                         [M+K]+ 354.041

Why the grouping matters

Because a long rule list connects almost anything, voting is only meaningful inside groups of features that are already known to belong together: same retention time, correlated intensities across samples, similar peak shapes. That evidence comes from groupFeatures(). IonFamilies adds the chemical interpretation on top. Good groups give good hints.
